summary: This specification extends Proxy Mobile IPv6 so a mobile access gateway can register more than one proxy care-of address with the local mobility anchor and set up multiple tunnels at once. That lets it use all its available network connections.

eli5.summary: A phone can use Wi-Fi and a mobile network at the same time, like having two roads to the same place and using both.

questions: how can pmipv6 use multiple access networks
what is the mag multipath binding option
how does pmipv6 use multiple tunnels
what is status code 180 in pmipv6
per flow vs per packet traffic distribution
subtitle: Lets a Proxy Mobile IPv6 gateway register several access links at once and keep a tunnel open over each.

tldr.problem: Base Proxy Mobile IPv6 lets a mobile access gateway register only one proxy care-of address with the local mobility anchor, so only one tunnel can be used at a time even when the gateway has LTE and WLAN links.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC adds a MAG Multipath Binding option and a MAG Identifier option to the binding messages, plus a new status code, so the gateway can register one binding per access link and the anchor keeps them all.
tldr.outcome: A gateway and its anchor can spread a mobile node's traffic over several tunnels, per flow or per packet, with a clean fallback when the anchor does not support the feature.

today: RFC 8278 is a Proposed Standard published in January 2018, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Multipath for Proxy Mobile IPv6
sections.content:
Using several access networks at once (multihoming) can bring redundancy and fault recovery, load balancing, load sharing and preference settings. In Proxy Mobile IPv6 (PMIPv6) the MAG (mobile access gateway) is the default gateway for the end node, and the LMA (local mobility anchor) is the topological anchor point. An IP tunnel runs between them, and the end node's traffic is carried over it.

The catch is that the base protocol does not allow a MAG to register more than one proxy care-of address (pCoA) with the LMA. Only one MAG/LMA tunnel can be used at the same time. This RFC removes that limit by defining a multiple-pCoA extension.

The authors also want the extension to work with GRE tunneling (with the key extension of RFC 5845), UDP encapsulation for NAT traversal (RFC 5844), prefix delegation (RFC 7148) and the Vendor Specific Mobility Option (RFC 5094).
sections.eli5: A gateway with two connections, like Wi-Fi and a phone network, could only tell the home base about one of them. This RFC lets it tell about both.

sections.title: How the Call Flow Works
sections.content:
In the RFC's example the MAG has both WLAN and LTE interfaces and is configured for multihoming. It attaches to both networks and gets a different pCoA from each. It then sends a Proxy Binding Update (PBU) over the LTE access carrying the new MAG Multipath Binding (MMB) option and a MAG Network Access Identifier (MAG-NAI) option.

The LMA accepts the PBU, allocates a Home Network Prefix (HNP), creates a Binding Cache Entry (BCE) marked as multipath-capable, and answers with a Proxy Binding Acknowledgement (PBA). A tunnel is then created over LTE using any supported encapsulation mode.

The MAG repeats the exchange over WLAN, this time including the HNP it received earlier. The LMA updates its binding cache with a new mobility session for the MAG. The request may be for a physical mobile node attached to the MAG or for a logical mobile node, which is a configuration that is always enabled on the MAG.
sections.eli5: The gateway first tells the home base about road one and gets a tunnel. Then it tells about road two, mentions the same address it was given, and gets a second tunnel.

sections.title: Spreading Traffic Across Tunnels
sections.content:
Once a multipath binding exists there are several tunnels between the MAG and the LMA, and either side can use any one or more of them. The RFC does not recommend or define a specific distribution scheme, but it names two well-known approaches.

Per-flow distribution ties each IP flow to one tunnel. A flow is never split, though it can be moved from one tunnel to another. The policy is either statically configured on both ends or negotiated over PMIPv6 signaling, using the flow binding mechanisms of RFC 6089 and RFC 6088.

Per-packet distribution splits packets of a single flow across tunnels. The weights are outside the scope of the RFC; it mentions equal sharing for symmetric paths and weighted sharing (an n:m ratio) for links of different speeds. Implementations must watch for reordering, buffering and effects on application performance.
sections.eli5: With two roads you can send each whole truck down one road (per flow), or split one truck's boxes between both roads (per packet). Splitting is faster but the boxes may arrive out of order.

sections.title: The MAG Multipath Binding Option
sections.content:
This new mobility header option, type 63, is used in PBU and PBA messages. It asks the LMA to register the current care-of address as one of the many addresses through which the MAG can be reached, and it describes the access network behind that address.

  • If-ATT: an 8-bit access technology type, taken from the Access Technology Type registry defined in RFC 5213.
  • If-Label: an 8-bit label configured on the MAG's WAN interface. It identifies the type of interface for application-routing policies. The RFC's example is a Wi-Fi interface labelled 9 and an LTE interface labelled 11, and two similar interfaces may share a label.
  • Binding ID (BID): an 8-bit identifier for the binding. Permitted values are 1 through 254; 0 and 255 are reserved.
  • B flag (bulk re-registration): asks the LMA to update the lifetime of all the node's bindings.
  • O flag (registration overwrite): asks the LMA to replace all existing bindings with this one.

The B and O flags must not both be set to 1, and O must be 0 in de-registration requests. The reserved bits are set to zero by the sender and ignored by the receiver.
sections.eli5: The option is a small label stuck on each request: what kind of road this is, a nickname for it, and a number so the home base can tell the roads apart.

sections.title: MAG Identifier Option and Status Code
sections.content:
The MAG Identifier option (type 64) conveys the identity of the MAG in PBU and PBA messages. It has a one-byte Subtype that says what kind of identifier follows, taken from the Mobile Node Identifier Option Subtypes registry, a reserved byte, and a variable-length Identifier.

The RFC also defines the status code CANNOT_SUPPORT_MULTIPATH_BINDING, value 180. The LMA should use it in a PBA when it rejects a multipath request, for example because it does not support multipath binding.
sections.eli5: The identifier option is the gateway's name tag. The status code is the home base's way of saying, "Sorry, I can't do two roads."

sections.title: Signaling Rules
sections.content:
A MAG that wants multipath support must include the MAG Multipath Binding option in each PBU it sends through its different WAN interfaces, and the MAG Identifier option must also be present. If the MAG knows the LMA supports the feature, it can send the PBUs sequentially or concurrently. If it does not know, it should first probe with a multipath PBU on one path only, so that the LMA does not overwrite one path's binding with another's.

If the LMA supports multipath and enables it, it must include the Multipath Binding option, without the MAG-NAI option, in the PBA. A legacy LMA skips both options, processes the rest of the message under RFC 5213 and does not echo them; the MAG, seeing a PBA without the option, should disable multipath support for that node.

If the node is not authorized for multipath, the LMA rejects the request with status 180 and must echo the Multipath Binding option, again without the MAG-NAI option. The MAG should then disable multipath for the node.
sections.eli5: If you are not sure the home base understands two roads, try one first. If the answer does not mention it, just use one road like before.

sections.title: Security and IANA
sections.content:
The RFC says the new capability has no impact on protocol security. The two options are carried like any other mobility header option under RFC 5213, so they inherit its security guidelines, and the RFC concludes it does not weaken PMIPv6 or introduce new vulnerabilities.

IANA allocated type 63 to the MAG Multipath Binding option and type 64 to the MAG Identifier option from the Mobility Options registry, and assigned status value 180 from the Status Codes registry.
sections.eli5: The new labels travel the same safe way as old ones, so they do not open new holes.
